newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Indians try to identify dead, injured from haj fire.
newsitem.headline: Indians try to identify dead, injured from haj fire.

text.p: Indian officials and anxious pilgrims combed through hospitals in Saudi Arabia on Thursday, struggling to find missing relatives and establish how many citizens died in a fire that killed over 300 haj pilgrims.

Saudi Arabia said 343 Moslems performing the annual haj pilgrimage died and 1,290 were injured by the blaze which on Tuesday tore through a vast tent camp in the plain of Mena, about 11 km (seven miles) from the Islamic holy city of Mecca.

Diplomats said they feared over 100 of the dead were Indians. But they said identifying bodies and tracing the missing was a daunting task. The 80,000 Indians among the two million pilgrims on haj carried little identification and were constantly on the move between the holy sites, diplomats said.

"The number of Indian victims is in the three-figure range," India's ambassador to Riyadh Mohammad Hamad Ansari told Reuters. "A count has not been possible because there are such a great number of burnt and charred bodies."
"The only identification pilgrims wear is a band around their wrist, and that was destroyed in the fire," he said. "Identification is a major problem."

After the raging fire swept through 70,000 tents at Mena, hundreds of ambulances ferried the dead and injured to 12 nearby hospitals. Witnesses said many victims burnt to death, others suffocated from the deadly fumes while some were crushed by a stampede as panic gripped the pilgrims.
"We have administrative staff in the camps and hospitals trying to collect information on the victims, find out who is there, who is missing," Ansari said.
Some Indian pilgrims said they were shuttling from hospital to hospital in search of missing family members and friends.
Many of the Indians lying in hospital said they had lost members of their family in the chaos of the fire.

"We are missing seven family members," said Ruksana, sitting in her white haj robes at the bedside of her badly-burnt brother Younes. She said her four-year-old daughter had escaped with light injuries. Rocking the child on her lap, Ruksana gestured to her husband Aslam, confined to a hospital bed with his burns.
Many of the injured were so severely burnt they could not open their eyes. The skin of others, blackened by the flames, peeled off their limbs.
"I am looking for my relative, I have not seen her, she is missing," said another Indian pilgrim at An-Noor hospital, about seven km (four miles) from Mecca.

Witnesses said panic spread quickly with the fire, which they said was caused by exploding gas cylinders. Riyadh has not given a cause for the blaze, but said investigations had shown it was not arson.
Ismail, a 28-year-old Indian pilgrim, said: "The fire started from a gas cylinder in an area close to my tent. I think about 500 were killed, most of them were Indians. They were burnt to death."
"Many of them were old people who couldn't flee fast enough. The tents were close to each other so the fire quickly spread from one tent to another," he said.
Indian embassy staff said they had been flooded with calls from worried relatives in Saudi Arabia and back home who were trying to find out if their family members were still alive.
"The difficulty is that since the day before yesterday, a mass of humanity has been on the move, performing the rituals of haj," an embassy official said.
"Saudi authorities said they will release the bodies of victims to the embassy after Eid...maybe early next week," said another. "We will not know the exact figure until Saudi authorities inform us."
Ambassador Ansari said the Indian pilgrim community was devastated by the fire and the uncertainty about the fate of those missing.
"Many are mourning for the dead, others are very anxious because they don't know who is alive and who is dead," he said.

The blaze was the latest tragedy to strike the pilgrimage to Mecca. Able-bodied Moslems are obliged to perform haj at least once if they can afford it. In 1990, 1,426 pilgrims were crushed to death in a stampede in a tunnel and in 1994, 270 pilgrims died in another stampede.
